memory_update.text: PWR should remain the reference benchmark for this node because it is the scaled public leader in electric T&D, substations, large-load infrastructure, and craft-led field execution.

MYRG is a high-relevance underfollowed candidate for utility T&D crew and substation construction exposure; next layer should verify current backlog, MSA mix, segment margins, and customer concentration.

PRIM is a high-relevance underfollowed candidate for power delivery, utility T&D, renewables interconnection, and MSA-backed infrastructure services, but execution risk and fixed-price exposure require close review.
WLDN belongs in the speculative shadow lane as a planning, optimization, inspection, compliance, and utility-program bottleneck candidate rather than a physical EPC crew provider.
Public pure-play vegetation-management candidates appear limited; Davey Tree is relevant operationally but was excluded from the candidate list because it is not a standard US-listed equity.
MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed electrical utility T&D contractor with direct exposure to transmission, distribution, substation, and renewable electrical infrastructure work.

PRIM should be tracked as an underfollowed power-delivery and utility infrastructure contractor with direct exposure to installation, maintenance, repair, substation, transmission, distribution, and storm-restoration work.

WLDN should be tracked as a second-order grid-services candidate focused on utility programs, demand response, energy efficiency, grid resiliency, and planning software rather than hard EPC construction.

Quanta Services remains the scaled reference leader for this node and should be used as the benchmark for backlog quality, labor availability, margin structure, utility relationships, and investor attention.

Utility vegetation management is strongly relevant to grid reliability and storm hardening, but the clearest specialists found in this pass, including Asplundh, ACRT, and Davey Tree, appear private or employee-owned; public-market exposure may require broader contractors or adjacent software/service firms.
MYRG should remain in the grid EPC/testing/field-services universe as a direct T&D and substation services candidate with backlog and master-service-agreement evidence to verify.

PRIM should remain in the universe as a diversified contractor with explicit power-delivery and utility installation/maintenance exposure; later layers must separate electric utility upside from gas, communications, and project-execution noise.
NVEE is a lower-attention second-order candidate for testing, inspection, commissioning, geospatial electric-utility data, and infrastructure asset-lifecycle services; materiality needs verification.

Vegetation-management pure plays appear sparse in US-listed equities; many relevant firms such as tree-trimming or utility vegetation-management contractors may be private or buried inside diversified service providers. Future passes should search BrightView, specialty environmental services, and utility O&M subcontractor disclosures.

Willdan Group was identified as a possible adjacent grid-optimization, utility-program, electrification, and LoadSEER software candidate but was excluded due to the four-candidate cap; consider in a later software/data and demand-side grid-services node.
MYRG should be retained for deeper Layer 2 work as a cleaner underfollowed electrical construction/T&D contractor with explicit backlog and utility grid exposure.

PRIM should be retained as a mixed but relevant utility services contractor where the key diligence question is whether power delivery is becoming a durable margin and backlog driver versus gas/communications/renewables cyclicality.

NVEE is a speculative-shadow candidate for the engineering, commissioning, substation design, utility coordination, and inspection layer; exposure appears real but may be too small or too diversified without segment-level confirmation.
The investable chokepoint for this node appears to split into two subnodes: craft-skilled field construction capacity and technical commissioning/design/inspection capacity.

Vegetation-management exposure remains difficult to map to US-listed equities because major players such as Asplundh and Davey are private; future passes should search for public roll-ups, utility O&M contractors, herbicide suppliers, LiDAR/geospatial inspection vendors, and storm-response subcontractors.
